newsitem.title: ITALY: Venice belltower separatists go on trial.
newsitem.headline: Venice belltower separatists go on trial.

text.p: Eight Italians who occupied the St Mark's Square bell tower in Venice in a separatist stunt went on trial on Wednesday but the case was adjourned after two hours until June 3.
The men appeared before a court in the town of Mestre, outside the lagoon city, in a high security building specially constructed for the trial of left-wing urban guerrillas in the early 1980s.
The men, who could be jailed for up to 25 years if convicted, face charges ranging from illegal possession of firearms, threatening public officials and illegally occupying church property.

Wearing jeans and tracksuits, they were led into cages before being allowed to sit in a row at the front of the courtroom close to their lawyers. One of the men used crutches after suffering injuries during the incident.

The eight, who hijacked a "vaporetto" ferry in the early hours of May 9 to take them and a ramshackle armoured vehicle down the Grand Canal to St Mark's, were arrested after only a few hours when police stormed the landmark and ended the sit-in.
The protesters issued a statement shortly before their arrest declaring themselves soldiers of the "Most Serene Republic" of Venice, for centuries a maritime power before its fall 200 years ago.
Judge Graziana Campanato rejected a plea from defence lawyers to free the defendants for the duration of the trial.

After spending half an hour in closed session with a panel of six lay assessors to consider the plea, Campanato read out her decision to shouts of "Send them home" and "Free Venice" from sympathisers. Relatives of the defendants packed the court.
Campanato later accepted a plea from lawyers for more time to prepare their case and ordered the adjournment of the trial until early next month.
The St Mark's protest appeared to strike a chord in northeast Italy, where frustration with central government bureaucracy and high taxes has been building for years.
Sympathisers wearing the insignia on their shirts of a group called the Free Federalist Entrepreneurs of Europe were in the court room on Wednesday.
The group, made up of northern businessmen, opened a bank account in the city of Padua to receive contributions for a legal defence fund for the eight men.
The group accuses the Rome government of strangling business in northeast Italy with high taxes and red tape.
One of the defendants, Antonio Barison, said in a newspaper interview from his cell on the eve of the trial that he expected no sympathy from the court.

"The judges will show no mercy with us, they will not let us off lightly. This is a state which is weak with the mighty and mighty in its treatment of the weak," he told Milan's Corriere della Sera on Wednesday.
